claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is initially a single-phase FCC crystal at 300 K.
The initial crystal contains a low density of pre-existing vacancy clusters.
The initial crystal contains solute inhomogeneities.
Yield-strength insensitivity over 10^8–10^10 s^-1 arises because nucleation is controlled by local chemical-potential barriers rather than dislocation-motion or annihilation kinetics.
Shockley partial dislocations nucleate preferentially at vacancy clusters.
Shockley partial dislocations nucleate preferentially at solute-rich precipitates.
Local lattice distortion at vacancy clusters or solute-rich regions lowers the critical stress for Shockley-partial emission.
Dislocation nucleation is athermal and controlled by a local reduction of the Peierls barrier at vacancy clusters.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
<11-1> loading has a higher resolved-shear-stress factor on the primary {111}<112> slip system than <110> loading.
The larger resolved-shear-stress factor under <11-1> loading delays nucleation until a higher macroscopic stress is reached.
<11-1> loading has a higher critical stacking-fault-energy barrier than <110> loading.
The yield stress under <11-1> loading will be approximately 15–20% higher than under <110> loading.
The yield-associated stress drop will coincide with Shockley-partial emission from vacancy clusters.
The HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults rather than a bulk HCP phase.
The intrinsic stacking faults are stabilized by the high stacking-fault energy of Cr-rich local environments.
HCP-coordinated atoms will remain confined to stacking-fault ribbons without a continuous HCP region growing beyond the fault width.
A continuous HCP-coordinated region extending more than 2 nm beyond a single-fault width would indicate a true phase transformation.
A stable HCP phase should exhibit a deep local-energy well, whereas an intrinsic stacking fault should exhibit a shallow well.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes 'athermal thermal activation,' the mechanism calls nucleation athermal, and the boundary states that thermal activation is significant. The role of thermal activation is therefore internally inconsistent.

A higher resolved-shear-stress factor is said to delay nucleation and produce a higher macroscopic yield stress. For a fixed critical resolved shear stress, a larger geometric projection would ordinarily reach that critical shear stress at a lower applied stress, so the stated geometric cause conflicts with the predicted direction unless an independently larger critical barrier is established.
The initial state affirmatively specifies pre-existing vacancy clusters, while the uncertainty field states that these features may instead be dynamic solute clusters rather than static vacancies.
